reference.source: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice
clinicalPearls: Results from infarction of the lateral pons, most often in the territory of the anterior inferior cerebellar artery arising from the basilar artery
Ipsilateral facial weakness, hearing loss, and vertigo follow involvement of the facial and vestibulocochlear nerve nuclei and fibres
Ipsilateral limb ataxia reflects damage to the middle cerebellar peduncle and cerebellar input
A crossed sensory pattern occurs with ipsilateral facial and contralateral body loss of pain and temperature from trigeminal and spinothalamic involvement
Ipsilateral Horner syndrome may arise from disruption of descending sympathetic fibres
Sudden unilateral deafness is a distinguishing feature because the labyrinthine artery commonly arises from the anterior inferior cerebellar artery
Motor power is usually preserved as the corticospinal tract lies more medially in the basis pontis
reference.pathophysiology: Lateral pontine syndrome follows ischaemia of the lateral pontine tegmentum and adjacent cerebellum, supplied chiefly by the anterior inferior cerebellar artery, a branch of the basilar artery. The infarct affects the facial nucleus and nerve (ipsilateral facial weakness), the vestibulocochlear nucleus and often the labyrinthine artery territory (vertigo and ipsilateral hearing loss), the trigeminal nucleus and crossing spinothalamic tract (ipsilateral facial and contralateral body sensory loss), the middle cerebellar peduncle (ipsilateral ataxia), and the descending sympathetic fibres (Horner syndrome). The medial location of the corticospinal tract usually spares limb strength, giving a crossed brainstem picture analogous to Wallenberg syndrome but at pontine level and with prominent auditory involvement.
additionalDifferentials: Cerebellopontine angle lesion such as vestibular schwannoma
Sudden sensorineural hearing loss of peripheral origin
additionalInvestigations: Diffusion-weighted MRI of the lateral pons and cerebellum to confirm the infarct
MR or CT angiography of the basilar artery and its cerebellar branches
Audiometry and vestibular testing to characterise the auditory and balance deficit
HINTS bedside oculomotor examination to distinguish central from peripheral vertigo
Cardiovascular and stroke risk workup including ECG and metabolic profiling
Vessel wall imaging where basilar atherosclerosis or dissection is suspected
redFlags: Progressive drowsiness or brainstem compression from associated cerebellar swelling
Evolving basilar thrombosis with risk of extensive pontine infarction
Central vertigo misattributed to a peripheral cause and discharged
New long-tract or bulbar signs suggesting medial extension
reference.prognosis: Vertigo and facial weakness often improve over weeks, but ipsilateral hearing loss may be permanent and cerebellar ataxia can persist; outcome is generally favourable unless the infarct is large or heralds basilar disease.
pitfalls: Attributing acute vertigo and hearing loss to a peripheral labyrinthine cause and missing the stroke
Overlooking a subtle Horner syndrome that helps localise the lesion
Confusing lateral pontine with lateral medullary syndrome when auditory signs are not sought
Assuming preserved limb power excludes a significant brainstem infarct
references: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice
Adams and Victor's Principles of Neurology
management: Manage as an acute basilar-territory stroke with thrombolysis within the window then antiplatelet therapy, imaging for basilar atherosclerosis or dissection
Start secondary prevention with antiplatelet or anticoagulant therapy, statin, and aggressive vascular risk-factor control
Protect against aspiration with swallow assessment and modified feeding while facial weakness and bulbar dysfunction persist
Treat vertigo, nausea, and vomiting with vestibular sedatives and antiemetics
Manage sudden sensorineural hearing loss with audiological rehabilitation, and protect the eye in facial-nerve palsy with lubrication and taping
Deliver multidisciplinary rehabilitation with physiotherapy for cerebellar ataxia and speech and swallow therapy
Monitor for evolving basilar disease and posterior-fossa swelling, escalating to neurosurgery if brainstem compression develops
